catalog_quote: [Ribeiro 2006:19, 'Phonology'] The primary stress falls ordinarily on the last syllable of a stem (4a). Secondary stress is generally assigned on an iambic, right-to-left pattern to every other syllable (4b). [(4a) wa-riOrE 1-child 'my child'; (4b) wa-riOrE-riOrE 1-child-child 'my grandchild'] As the examples show, in order to fit the iambic pattern, the original stress pattern of a stem may be rearranged under compounding (4b), as well as under suffixation, since all derivational suffixes are stressed. On the other hand, a number of grammatical and discourse morphemes – including tense and aspect markers (4c), the indefinite article =dõ, =õ (5a), and most postpositions (5b) – are unstressed, and thus do not alter the stress of the stem to which they attach: [(4c) wa-riOrE=r-e 1-child=CTFG-IMPRF '(he, she) is my child'; (5a) wÈhÈ=dõ arrow=INDEF 'an arrow'; (5b) wÈhÈ=dI arrow=INSTR 'with arrow'] ... [p.18] As we will see, a typical finite verb in Karajá presents tense-aspect clitics, which are unstressed. In independent clauses, the stress falls ordinarily on the last syllable of the verb stem (1). In relative clauses, however, the stress shifts to the tense-aspect clitic (2).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and final within the stem/derived word: primary stress on the last syllable of the stem (derivational suffixes count as part of the stressed domain and take the stress), with enclitics (tense-aspect markers, indefinite article, most postpositions) outside the stress domain; secondary stresses alternate leftward from the primary (iambic, right-to-left). Corroborated in Portuguese by Ribeiro 2001/2002 p.76: 'A posição do acento é predizível, recaindo geralmente sobre a última sílaba da palavra' and p.80 'acento fixo na última sílaba'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is generally assigned on an iambic, right-to-left pattern to every other syllable' (p.19), e.g. wa-riore-riore [ˌwariˌoreˌrioˈre] 'my grandchild'.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Tense-aspect clitics, the indefinite article and most postpositions are unstressed, but 'become stressed when attached to monosyllabic stems' (p.23 fn.6: he=di 'with firewood' [heˈdi], r-a=kre 'he will go' [raˈkre]); the imperfective =r-e becomes stressed before the future marker. (ii) Grammatical 'stress shift': in relative/subordinate clauses stress moves from the stem-final syllable onto the tense-aspect clitic (p.18: [doroˈde] 'the White man who arrived' vs [doˈrode] 'the White man arrived'), the basic marker of subordination.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem plus derivational suffixes (the 'phonological word characterized by a single primary stress', Ribeiro 2002: 481); enclitics are extrametrical except after monosyllabic hosts and under subordination stress shift. Ribeiro 2001/2002 phrases the same generalization at word level ('última sílaba da palavra'). Examples are given in phonetic transcription of words/short phrases; female-speech forms are the citation standard.
new_statements.identity_note: Ribeiro's statements cover Karajá as a whole (four dialects: Southern Karajá, Northern Karajá, Javaé, Xambioá; he notes they 'share basically the same phonological system'); his examples are mainly Southern/Northern Karajá female speech. Glottolog kara1500 = the language-level node; Javaé (java1245) and Xambioá are dialects under it.

new_statements.quote: Im Auslaut stehen in den Regel kurze Vocale, welche den Wortaccent tragen; nicht als eigentlich auslautende Konsonanten sind die n (ñ) und m aufzufassen, welche wohl nur die Nasalierung des vorhergehenden Vocales andeuten sollen. [p. 173] || Diadem: ödĭdăe; wiederum mit Kürzung, wahrscheinlich weil hier das Wort dreisilbig geworden ist und der Accent auf der letzten Silbe liegt.) [p. 156] || ...wird über *yadooma zu E. yadôma, Kr. yādŏmă, wobei es zweifelhaft bleibt, ob der (ungewöhnliche) Accent auf der Contraktionssilbe ein Aequivalent für die Längung bedeutet. [p. 176]
new_statements.translation: In word-final position there stand as a rule short vowels, which carry the word accent; the n (ñ) and m are not to be taken as genuinely final consonants, they presumably only indicate the nasalisation of the preceding vowel. [p. 173] || Diadem: ödĭdăe; again with shortening, probably because here the word has become trisyllabic and the accent lies on the last syllable.) [p. 156] || ...becomes, via *yadooma, E. yadôma, Kr. yādŏmă, where it remains doubtful whether the (unusual) accent on the contraction syllable is an equivalent for the lengthening. [p. 176]

(the paragraph begins with italic 'Im Auslaut' inside the consonant section, after item…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's final-syllable rule and with Ribeiro 2006 ('primary stress falls ordinarily on the last syllable of a stem'). It is a century-older, second-hand (transcription-based) confirmation of final word accent; it adds nothing on secondary stress or clitics. The 1919 JSA article listed in the catalog could not be downloaded (Persée PDF altcha-protected; only the first page preview), but its readable first page is verbatim the opening of the 1916 IAE paper and its title is the 1916 paper's section heading (IAE p. 149 'Die Phonetik der Karajásprache'), so the quotes were taken from the open archive.org copy of the 1916 version that the citation bundles.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the final syllable: Kunike states that words normally end in a short vowel and that this final vowel bears the word accent; he treats final-syllable accent as the default (a word that becomes trisyllabic gets accent on its last syllable) and calls accent on a non-final contraction syllable 'unusual'. No stress section as such; the statements are asides inside the sound-by-sound treatment (vowel contraction, final consonants), based on Krause's, Ehrenreich's, Castelnau's and Coudreau's transcriptions rather than Kunike's own fieldwork.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 176: an 'unusual' accent on a contraction syllable in yadôma / yādŏmă 'girl' (men's-speech contraction of women's yadokoma), which Kunike tentatively links to compensatory lengthening. p. 148 quotes Krause on the intonation ('Der Tonfall ist etwas singend', with syllables sometimes drawn out) - an impressionistic remark, not a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Kunike treats the Karajá of Goyaz as three subgroups (Šambioá, Javahé/Šavajé, and Karajá proper) and cites forms from all of them (Krause's 'Kr. Savajé' vs 'Kr. Karajá', Ehrenreich, Castelnau, Coudreau, Kissenberth); the accent statements are made for the language as a whole, with men's vs women's speech distinguished but no dialect restriction on the stress remark.
